primary.evidence: Must recognize NH3 has H bonded to N and therefore hydrogen bonds, unlike NF3.
Must identify dipole-dipole attractions as the main intermolecular force in NF3, which has no N-H bond.

supporting.evidence: Identifying dipole-dipole forces in NF3 requires recognizing that the trigonal pyramidal NF3 molecule is polar.

primary.evidence: Must explain the higher boiling point of NH3 (240 K vs 144 K) by the greater strength of its intermolecular attractions.

supporting.evidence: The explanation rests on hydrogen bonding in NH3 outweighing the forces in NF3 despite NF3 having more electrons.

primary.evidence: Must identify the bonding in KCl and NaCl as ionic.
Must account for NaCl melting higher than KCl through stronger lattice attraction from the smaller Na+ ion at equal charge.
Must identify that the valence electrons of Si, P and Cl are in the n = 3 level from their electron configurations.
Must explain the increasing first ionization energy from Si to P to Cl shown in the table.

supporting.evidence: The explanation requires increasing nuclear charge with electrons added to the same shell, giving stronger attraction to the valence electrons.

primary.evidence: Must identify the element (Cu) from an average atomic mass lying between isotope masses 62.93 and 64.93 amu.
Must decide which isotope is more abundant from where the weighted-average atomic mass lies relative to the two isotope masses.
